newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: ANALYSIS-LITHUANIA CURRENCY BOARD END STARTS FEARS.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-LITHUANIA CURRENCY BOARD END STARTS FEARS.

text.p: Lithuania's currency board, the linchpin of the Baltic country's economic stability, is becoming a source of anxiety as the country makes plans to scrap it, analysts say.
Critics of the mechanism, which pegs the Lithuanian litas to the dollar at a rate of four to one, say the currency is overvalued and it hampers the country's exports.
The Lithuanian government itself says the currency board peg has led to an inflexible monetary system and that it will gradually replace it with a classical central bank system.
The central bank says that even after the currency board is abolished, the peg to the dollar will continue until 1999.
"The currency board structure, having the litas pegged to the dollar, is a positive thing for investors," said Petri Karjalainen, head of investment house Williams de Broe's Baltics division.

"Our preference would be that they would stick to their currency board because it has been a good structure in Estonia and has been one of the basis for the developments in the economy," Karjalainen, based in Helsinki, told Reuters.
The system also exists in Baltic cousin Estonia, where the Estonian kroon is fixed at eight kroon to one German mark.
Economists agree currency boards in both countries have helped stabilised their economies since the shock of quitting the Soviet Union.
Lithuania's annual inflation rate plunged from almost 1,200 percent in 1992 to 35.7 percent in 1995 and 13.1 percent in 1996. A similar scenario applies to Estonia.
"It forces the central bank to be more disciplined," said Gunnar Tersman, economist at Sweden's Handelsbanken.
"It also foces the budget to be more responsibly managed and this has been a problem, especially in Lithuania," he said.
Lithuania has not reaped economic benefits from being close to Finland as Estonia has or had the advantage of Latvia, whose central bank governor Einars Repse is hawkish on currency stability.
"Lithuania is much more prone to political infighting. The whole place is less stable and therefore they need a currency board," said Tersman.
U.S. credit ratings agency Moody's economist Sosi Vartanesyan, based in New York, said it was unlikely abolishing the currency board would wreck any financial havoc.

"In the case of Lithuania it has served several purposes in terms of stabilising the currency and bringing down inflation. But in the long run it probably can not be maintained since it does not allow for much flexibility," she told Reuters.

"Abolishing it would certainly bring in an element of uncertainty as far as the exchange rate is concerned. But it is not necessarily something that is good for the country. Investors will have to adjust," said Vartanesyan.
Tomas Lind, senior area manager for central and eastern Europe at Sweden's S-E-Banken, said scrapping the currency board would help Lithuania more than it would Estonia in the long run.
Estonian exports have a high percentage of imported components, with many companies assembling and producing products in Estonia but importing raw materials from outside, Lind said.
For this reason, devaluing the Estonian kroon would not boost exports significantly, Lind said.
"Then again the currency itself cannot boost the export industry," Lind warned.
Lind said a model with a crawling peg system, such as the one introduced in Poland, could not be ruled out for Lithuania if the government sought to float the litas.
This could be one way to quell investors' fears of instability if the currency board were to be abolished.
"I would not say that it would scare away investors -- look at Hungary and Poland," Lind said.
Tersman said Lithuania did not have the discipline needed for this type of system either.

"Given past history and looking at it from the point of view of financial markets, I think people would be sceptical that they could back this up with the necessary fiscal and monetary measures," he said.
But more than anything, investors are looking for stability and hope the government will not opt for overnight changes.
"We hope that the peg of litas at four to one for the dollar will stay," said Karjalainen.

"If and when it was to be changed we would hope that the government and the central bank will indicate very clearly how and when the shift will be done in order to not create uncertainty in the market," said Karjalainen.
"Much is at stake for these new countries and confidence could be ruined quite easily," said Heinz Sjogren, area manager for the Baltic countries at Swedbank.

"I hope that talks with the IMF (International Monetary Fund) will continue and when -- and if -- the change takes place that it will be done under IMF supervision and in an orderly way," said Sjogren.
